scenes.title: Cold open
narration: The Iron Spirit: The Militant Dance of Nago
This is Nago. 18th-21st century.

scenes.title: Where and when
narration: The dance originated from the syncretization of Yoruba orisha and rites during the Atlantic slave trade.
The term Nago stems from the historic exonym 'Anagó' used for the Yoruba.
It is now considered a nanchon (nation) of lwa within Haitian Vodou, with distinct practices still observed in Northern Haiti.

scenes.title: When it is danced
narration: Nago is performed to honor the Ogou spirits, who are masculine, militant, and powerful.
It is a ritualized expression of these spirits, often marking the beginning and end of ceremonies with the call 'Awo che Nago'.
Today it is a living tradition.

scenes.title: Listen
narration: The music requires three Rada cowhide-head drums.
Rhythms are categorized by tempo and intensity, specifically the fast 'Nago Chaud' and the slow, heavy 'Nago Grand Coup'.
Listen for the three Rada cowhide-head drums.
The music is driven by three Rada cowhide-head drums, alternating between fast-paced, high-energy rhythms and slow, heavy, grounding beats.

scenes.title: The costume and the setting
narration: The ritual setting is distinguished by the use of an iron 'zin' (ceremonial cooking pot) rather than the typical clay vessel.
The dance is performed within the context of Vodou ceremonies.

scenes.title: The people
narration: Loco is recognized as the 'king of the Nago' (wa Nago).
The Ogou spirits are the dominant group within the Nago nanchon.
Veneration of the Nago as a wholly distinct nation is more typical of Northern Haitian Vodou, whereas in other areas it is increasingly absorbed into Rada or Petwo rites.
The Nago nanchon is a religious syncretization of Yoruba orisha and rites, sharing historical roots with Candomblé Ketu in Brazil and Santería in Cuba.

scenes.title: Family tree

Nago is sibling of Petwo: Nago lwa are sometimes incorporated into Petwo rites.

scenes.title: A respectful note
narration: Nago is a sacred ritual tradition within Haitian Vodou. Outsiders should be aware that rituals are religious ceremonies and should be approached with respect for the practitioners' customs, including the use of specific ritual objects like the iron zin.
